title: Why can Kafka sustain very high throughput on commodity disks: explain sequential append-only writes vs random I/O, zero-copy transfer (`sendfile`), and reliance on the OS page cache rather than an in-process cache.
shortTitle: Why can Kafka sustain very high throughput on commodity disks?
keyPoints: Sequential append-only writes are 1-2 orders of magnitude faster than random I/O on both HDDs and SSDs.
Zero-copy transfer (sendfile / FileChannel.transferTo) ships bytes from page cache to socket without JVM heap copies.
Kafka relies on the OS page cache instead of an in-process cache, keeping the JVM heap small and GC pauses short.
Recent data is already in the page cache from being written, so tail consumers are served from memory for free.
The page cache survives broker process restarts, so a restarted broker serves hot data immediately.
Zero-copy is bypassed when TLS encryption or message-format down-conversion is needed.
Durability comes from replication and the acks contract, not from fsync per message.

s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka is fast on cheap disks because it writes sequentially to an append-only log, serves reads with zero-copy sendfile straight from page cache to socket, and leans on the OS page cache instead of an in-process cache.
s1_definition.profdef:
Kafka achieves very high throughput on commodity hardware through three reinforcing design choices.

- **Sequential append-only writes** – producers only append to the end of the active segment, so the disk sees large contiguous writes instead of scattered random I/O.
- **Zero-copy transfer** – consumer reads use the OS `sendfile` system call (Java's `FileChannel.transferTo`) to move bytes directly from the page cache to the network socket without copying through the JVM heap.
- **OS page cache** – Kafka stores no in-process cache; the OS caches recently written segment data in memory, serving tail consumers from RAM for free.
- **Small JVM heap** – because the cache is in the kernel, the broker runs with a small heap, keeping garbage-collection pauses short and predictable.
- **Warm restarts** – the page cache survives a process restart, so a restarted broker serves recent data from memory immediately.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India records every transaction in a long ledger. Instead of flipping around the ledger to find a spot for each entry (random I/O), clerks always write the next entry on the very next line at the end (sequential append), which is fast and smooth. When head office asks for a copy of recent pages, instead of a clerk photocopying each page and walking it over, the bank uses a direct pass-through chute from the shelf to the courier (zero-copy). And because the most recent pages are already lying open on the desk from being written, anyone who wants them just reads them off the desk instead of fetching from the vault (page cache).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Three Pillars of Kafka Throughput

  1. Sequential Append-Only Writes
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Active Segment (append-only)               │
  │  [rec1][rec2][rec3][rec4] → → → [recN]     │
  │  Disk head moves in one direction only      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  2. Zero-Copy Transfer (sendfile)
  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐
  │ Segment   │───→│ Page     │───→│ Network  │
  │ File      │    │ Cache    │    │ Socket   │
  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘
       No copy through JVM heap!

  3. OS Page Cache
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  JVM Heap: 6 GB (small, short GC)        │
  │  OS Page Cache: 58 GB (hot segments)     │
  │  Disk: cold data only                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Combined Data Path:
  Producer ──append──→ Segment ──→ Page Cache
                                       │
  Consumer ──fetch──→ sendfile ────────┘──→ Socket ──→ NIC
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka sustains very high throughput on commodity disks because of three reinforcing design choices. Sequential append-only writes mean the disk sees large contiguous blocks instead of scattered random operations, which is one to two orders of magnitude faster. Zero-copy transfer using the sendfile system call ships bytes directly from the OS page cache to the network socket without copying through the JVM, letting one broker feed many consumers at near network line rate. And relying on the OS page cache instead of an in-process cache keeps the JVM heap small, GC pauses short, and recent data served from RAM for free.

On the National Bank of India card-authorization stream, this is exactly why cheap servers with ordinary SSDs kept up with millions of events per second. The writes were sequential batched appends, the hot tail was served from the page cache, and zero-copy let one broker fan those events out to the fraud scorer, the ledger updater, and analytics without saturating CPU.

The nuances that matter in production are that zero-copy is bypassed when the broker must transform bytes, such as with TLS encryption or message-format down-conversion for old clients, so keep client and broker formats aligned and budget CPU for encryption. Durability comes from replication and the acks contract rather than fsync per message. And because Kafka leans on the page cache, you size the broker with a small heap and plenty of free RAM rather than a giant heap that starves the cache.

Remember one sentence: Kafka wins by turning messaging into sequential log appends and cached, zero-copy reads, which is the pattern commodity hardware is best at.
